newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Burundi follows Kabila in rejecting U.N. rights reps.
newsitem.headline: Burundi follows Kabila in rejecting U.N. rights reps.

text.p: Burundi, following the example of Congo leader Laurent Kabila, has rejected the U.N. human rights investigator assigned to that country for the past two years, diplomats said on Thursday.

In a letter to the United Nations on July 11, Burundi's Foreign Minister Luc Rukingama said that Paulo Sergio Pinheiro, a leading Brazilian human rights authority, produced slanted and politically inspired reports.

Rukingama also said that Pinheiro, the investigator, based his reports on unproven allegations and had not visited the country since Burundi's Tutsi military ruler Pierre Buyoya took power in a coup one year ago, the envoys said.

In reply, Ralph Zacklin, the Geneva-based acting U.N. human rights commissioner, said decisions on investigators were up to the inter-governmental Commission on Human Rights. He noted the difficulties Pinheiro had in getting permission to visit Burundi and appealed to Burundi to allow another visit, according to the July 16 letter obtained by Reuters.

Rukingama was visiting U.N. headquarters in New York on July 16 and was presumed to have told U.N. officials then he wanted Pinheiro replaced, the envoys said. But the news surfaced on Thursday when a Security Council member asked U.N. officials to check on reports about Burundi's position.

Burundi's action follows that of President Laurent Kabila, who rejected Roberto Garreton of Chile as the special U.N. rapporteur probing alleged massacres of Rwandan Hutu refugees in the former Zaire by Kabila's supporters before he became president of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

In an effort to conduct the probe as quickly as possible, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, at the urging of U.S. Ambassador Bill Richardson, said he would appoint his own team, although he is having difficulties finding a team leader who is immediately available.

But U.N. officials at the time stressed this was an exception, approved by Security Council members, to get around the deadlock, and would not set a precedent. Diplomats said Annan was not expected to concede to Burundi's request.

Human rights groups, however, had warned about setting a precedent. Joanna Weschler, the U.N. representative for Human Rights Watch, told Richardson in a June 3 letter that allowing Kabila to change rapporteurs would prompt Rwanda and Burundi to follow suit.
"Garreton and Pinheiro are exceptionally good, among the best people the United Nations has, and this is painful for a government," she said in response to a query.
"Once you open the box you violate the principle that there are investigations a la carte and obviously the next government will do the same."

More than 200,000 Hutu and Tutsi civilians have been ordered into camps guarded by Burundian troops since last year. The army says the camps protect people against Hutu rebel attacks but Pinheiro said in March that authorities were "systemtically resettling rural populations using an outdated strategy of forces villagization."

Before the coup last July Pinheiro criticised extremist Hutu rebels as well as the Tutsi-dominated army, complaining of a paralysis in the country's weak coalition government and a biased and lax judiciary.
